title: Checkpoint 6: Hans vs Stockfish (skill 0)
notes: Checkpoint after game 6, from the Italian Game: Hans plays the yardstick, Stockfish at skill 0. Nothing is studied afterwards.

moves.thought: This is the Giuoco Piano, and 5.d4 is the main line: Black's best is 5...exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Nc3, giving me a strong central duo and fast development. The tactical try 5...Nxe4 fails to 6.dxc5 or 6.d5, and 5...exd4 6.cxd4 Nxe4 runs into 7.d5 hitting the knight with tempo.

Black's 5...Be7 is passive, so I can grab space in the center with d5, hitting the c6 knight — Nb4 loses a piece to cxb4, so the knight must retreat to b8 or go offside to a5 where Bd3 leaves it stranded. The alternative dxe5 Nxe4 releases the tension and invites counterplay, so the space-gaining push is clearly better.

My c4 bishop is attacked by the knight on a5, so I must move it; Bb3 invites Nxb3 doubling my pawns, while Bd3 keeps the bishop, reinforces e4, and leaves Black's knight stranded on the rim with no good way back. No Black captures or checks are available after Bd3.

Black's e5 pawn is actually undefended — the bishop retreated to e7 and the knight on f6 doesn't cover it — so Nxe5 simply wins a pawn. If Black counters with Qd6 I play Nc4, trading off the offside knight on a5 while the bishop recaptures and guards d5; if 8...Nxe4 9.Bxe4 or 8...Nxd5 9.exd5 I stay a pawn up.

I'm a clean pawn up and Black's knight on a5 is offside and loose, so b4 gains a tempo by kicking it — if it goes to c4 I can take with the knight (Nxc4 bxc4 Bxc4) to keep my strong bishop and win a second pawn. Nxe4 ideas fail to Bxe4, leaving the a5 knight still harassed.

I'm a clean pawn up, and my e5 knight has no safe aggressive outpost — Nc4 loses to bxc4, Nc6 loses to dxc6, and Nxf7/Nxd7 just drop a piece for a pawn. So I retreat with Nf3, keeping the extra pawn, defending e4 chains with Bd3, and preparing to castle quickly while Black's knight on b7 stays passive.

I'm a clean pawn up and Black's 10...c6 challenges my d5 wedge, so I want to reinforce the center rather than release it with dxc6 (which would activate the b7 knight against b4). After 11.c4 bxc4 12.Bxc4 cxd5 13.exd5 my d5 pawn is held by the bishop and queen and I keep the extra pawn plus a strong passer; 11...c5 12.bxc5 Bxc5 13.cxb5 also leaves me a pawn ahead.

Black has just taken on c4, so the simplest and best move is to recapture with the bishop, regaining the pawn and keeping the strong b3-g8 diagonal while supporting my d5 wedge. If Black answers cxd5, I take with the bishop and after Nxd5 exd5 I get a healthy passed d-pawn with Black's knight stuck on b7.

I must answer the check on b4, and blocking with Bd2 is cleanest: after Bxd2+ I recapture with Nbxd2, developing a piece, keeping my pawn structure intact and my strong bishop on c4 plus the d5/e4 center. Nc3 invites Bxc3+ damaging my queenside pawns, and moving the king forfeits castling.

Black's bishop on b4 is attacked by my dark-squared bishop, and resolving the tension now suits me: after Bxb4 axb4 Black's b4 pawn is isolated and weak, his knight on b7 stays passive, and I keep the strong d5/e4 pawn duo with easy development (Nbd2 or Qb3 covering a2, then castling). Alternatives like O-O allow Nxe4 complications, so I prefer the clean trade.

Black's immediate threat is ...Nxe4, since my e-pawn is currently undefended, and Nc3 fails to ...bxc3 with no recapture. Nbd2 develops the last knight, guards e4, and keeps d5 adequately supported (after ...cxd5 Bxd5 Nxd5 Qxd5 the trades are even and my queen lands actively), while the knight can later head for c4 or b3 to hit the loose b4 pawn.

My bishop on c4 is attacked by the knight on a5, but instead of retreating I can use a tactic: 16.dxc6 Nxc4 17.cxd7+ is check, so after 17...Bxd7 18.Nxc4 I've traded my d-pawn for two of Black's pawns and emerge a clean pawn up. If Black replies 16...dxc6 instead, then 17.Qa4 hits both the a5 knight and the loose c6 pawn, again winning material.

My c6 pawn is doomed to ...dxc6, so I should trade it off favourably first: cxd7+ removes Black's d-pawn with check, and then Nxc4 recaptures the knight that took my bishop, leaving me a clean pawn up with a 4-v-3 kingside majority. If Black answers 17...Kxd7, his king is badly exposed and after Nxc4 I get strong initiative with Ne5/Qd4 ideas.

The black knight on c4 is completely undefended — the queen on d7 does not cover it — so Nxc4 simply wins a piece back, restoring material balance with an extra pawn. If Black tries 18...Qc6 hitting c4 and e4, 19. Qd4 defends both, and 18...Qxd1+ 19. Rxd1 leaves me a clean pawn up with the better structure.

Black's knight is eyeing my loose e4 pawn, so I want a move that defends it while gaining time — Nd6 does both, hitting the c8 bishop and sitting on a dominant square, and it's safely protected by my queen along the open d-file (Qxd6? Qxd6 wins the queen). If Black trades queens or retreats the bishop, I keep my extra pawn and can castle next.

I'm a pawn up and my knight on d6 is strong (it also tactically guards e4, since Nxe4 would just lose a piece to Nxe4). Castling develops the rook and keeps everything safe; if Black answers Rd8 I simply take the bishop with Nxc8 and consolidate with Qe2 protecting e4.

My knight on d6 is attacked twice (Qc7 and Rd8) and undefended, and defending with Qd4 fails to Qxd6! Qxd6 Rxd6 winning a piece. So I simply cash in with Nxc8, winning Black's undeveloped bishop and keeping my extra pawn in a simple position where a3 can later blunt the passed b-pawn.

My knight on c8 is doomed (Black's rook attacks it and every retreat square is covered by the queen or rook), so the priority is to snap off the hanging rook on d1 immediately — inserting Ne7+ only lets Black recapture with the queen on an active square hitting e4. I capture with the f1-rook so that Ra1 keeps defending a2 while my king still covers f2, leaving me two rooks and a knight against the queen and rook after ...Rxc8.

My knight on c8 is attacked by the rook on a8, so I must address it; Nb6 solves the problem with tempo by attacking the rook right back, and the knight then has a fine retreat to d5 (protected by Rd1, hitting c7 and b4). If Black tries Qc5 to double-attack, Nxa8 simply wins the rook, since after Qxf2+ Kh1 I have Rdf1 backed by Ra1.

I'm down a queen for a rook, so I need activity and traps rather than passivity. Rd4 centralizes, attacks the loose knight on e4 and the b4 pawn, and crucially baits Qxd4, which after Nxd4 would trade the queen for a rook and restore material balance; the rook on d4 is otherwise untouchable since only the queen can reach it.

Black's immediate threat is Ne2+, forking my king and the rook on d4, and I also need to keep a rook on the b6–f2 diagonal so ...Qxf2+ never comes — so most rook moves are out. Kh1 solves everything at once: Ne2 is no longer check (and Rd2 would then just hit the loose knight), ...Qb5+ ideas vanish, and my rook stays on d4 blocking the diagonal while pressuring b4 for a future a3 undermining of the c3 knight.

The knight on c3 is completely undefended (the b4 pawn attacks c3 rather than defending it), so Rc4 hits both the knight and the b4 pawn. If the knight runs I win the b-pawn, if Black defends with Ra3 or Rc8 I trade into a much healthier material balance, and Nxa2 just loses a piece to Rxa2.

I'm down material (two rooks and a knight against queen, rook and knight), so I want to grab the free b4 pawn and avoid piece trades that magnify Black's advantage; Rxb4 is safe since neither the queen on d6, the rook on a8, nor the knight on c3 covers b4. Alternatives like Rxc3 bxc3 or Rc8+ Rxc8 just liquidate my pieces and leave Black's queen dominant, while Rc5/Rc6/Rc7 all drop the rook to Qxc-something.

My rook on b4 is attacked by the queen and Black's knight on d1 is defended along the d-file, so Rxd1 Qxd1+ loses material. Rd4 saves the rook (defended by Nf3, so Qxd4 Nxd4 wins the queen for a rook) while doubling the attack on d1 — and if Black grabs with Nxf2+ Kg1, the knight is trapped since Rd4 covers d1, d3, e4 and g4.
Only one legal move is available — the knight check on f2 must be answered, and Kg1 is forced. After Kg1 the knight on f2 is attacked by my king, so Black must move it or it falls.

I'm actually down material here (queen+rook vs two rooks+knight), so declining the knight with Kh1 or Kf1 lets Black simply save it with Ng5 and stay a piece up. Taking with gxh3 restores near-equality; after 30...Qg3+ 31.Kh1 Qxh3 I can hold with Rd2, covering h2 and preparing Rg2 to block the f3-h1 diagonal, reaching a playable two-rooks-versus-queen endgame.

Black's Qe6 threatens Qe1+ followed by Qxa1, picking up a rook, so I must address that immediately. Rad1 moves the loose rook off a1, covers e1 (so Qe1 is simply met by Rxe1), doubles my rooks on the open d-file, and prepares invasion with Rd7; after Qxa2 I still get strong activity with Rd7 hitting g7.

With two rooks and a knight against the queen, I need coordination and no loose checks: R1d2 defends h2 (so Qxh2+ is impossible) while the rook on d4 covers the whole fourth rank, taking away Qg4+ and Qh4, leaving Black with no checks at all. The alternative Rd8+ would trade down into rook+knight vs queen, which is clearly worse, and knight moves like Ng5 or Ne5 simply drop a piece.

My rooks are doubled on the open d-file, which both keeps them mutually defended (so Black's Qe3+ fork never wins material) and means Black's rook can never land on d8 without being captured twice; meanwhile h2 is defensible because after Qg3+ I simply play Kh1 and Qxh2+ would be met by Kxh2. So I start my only real asset: the passed a-pawn, aiming for a5-a6 and then the Rd8+ trade combination to let it run.

Rf2 looks tempting as a block, but it abandons the d4 rook (Qxd4 simply wins a rook since Rd2 was its only defender), so I must step aside with the king while keeping the rooks mutually supporting. Kh1 tucks the king into the corner where only Qe1+ is available, after which Kg2 and my doubled rooks on the d-file stay coordinated and guard a4, with Rd8+ ideas in reserve.
Only one legal move is available — the king must step out of check to g2, since no piece can block or capture the queen on e1.

My rook on d4 can swing to d7 where it attacks Black's undefended queen along the seventh rank while being protected by Rd2, so Qxd7 Rxd7 would win the queen for a rook. That forces the queen to retreat (Qe2+ just loses to Rxe2) and gains me the active seventh rank plus pressure on g7, which is my best practical defense down material.

I'm material down, so I must keep my rooks connected and avoid any rook trade; Rd4 (from d2) attacks the queen while being defended by Rd7, so the queen must move. If Black answers 37...Rxa4 defending the queen, I can play 38.Rxb4 Rxb4 39.Rxg7+ and 40.Rxh7, reaching a nearly level rook-and-pawn ending.

My rook on d4 is attacked by the queen but defended by Rd7, and I'm down material, so I want to harass the queen while keeping my rooks connected. Rd3 hits the queen with a rook that's protected along the d-file (Qxd3 Rxd3 would win the queen for a rook), gaining a tempo and keeping my defensive battery intact. Rxg7+ fails because that rook would be undefended on g7.

Rd2 blocks the check, and crucially the rook on d2 is protected by my other rook down the open d-file (d7–d2 is clear), so Qxd2+ Rxd2 would trade Black's queen for a rook and leave me fine in the rook endgame. King moves instead let the queen keep checking for free, and on g2 I'd face Qe4+ ideas, so blocking with the defended rook is the most solid and active choice.

I'm down a queen for a rook, so my only practical hope is the perpetual rook activity on the d-file and 7th rank that has already produced two repetitions. Playing R2d3 again hits the queen on c3, keeps Rd7 hitting g7, and invites 40...Qb2+ 41.Rd2 Qc3 for a third repetition; alternatives like Rxg7+ or Rd8+ just trade off my activity and lose outright.

I'm down material (Black has queen+rook+3 pawns against my two rooks and two pawns), so my salvation is the repetition: Rd2 blocks the check on the second rank, the rook is safely defended by Rd7 (Qxd2+ Rxd2 leaves a drawn ending), and after Qc3 R2d3 Qb2+ I reach the position for a third time. King moves like Kf3 or Kg3 would let Black's queen escape with the extra material and start making real progress against my exposed king.

Rxg7+ fails to Kxg7 since after Rd7+ Kf8 I'm left with a lone rook against queen and pawns. Instead R2d5 attacks the queen while being protected by the rook on d7 (Qxd5+ Rxd5 wins the queen), gains a tempo, and keeps both rooks mutually defended and active, with Qd6/Qe7 also losing the queen to a rook capture.

Black's queen can't take on d5 since my rooks defend each other (Qxd5 Rxd5 reaches an equal rook ending), so my doubled rooks on d5/d7 form a solid barrier; my only real weakness is the h2 pawn falling to checks along the second rank. Playing h3 gives my king luft while the pawn stays permanently guarded by the king on g2, and any queen attempt to attack it along the d-file (Qd3) simply loses to Rxd3.

My two rooks defend each other on the d-file, so any queen fork only wins a rook at the cost of the queen; but Kh2 and Kg3 allow Qe5+/Qd6+ where I can't interpose, forcing the trade on favorable terms for Black. Kf1/Kf2 run into Qd3+/Qc5+ ideas too, while after Kg1 the checks like Qc5+ can be met by the blocking Rd4 (protected by Rd7), and Qe1+ Kg2 Qe4+ just repeats the position.

I must move the king, and I checked that both rooks defend each other on the d-file, so queen forks like Qe4+/Qd3+ win nothing. Kh2 gives Black the fewest checking resources (only Qf4+ or Qe2+), keeps my king next to the h3 pawn, and avoids the h1/g2 diagonal checks that would keep me shuffling.

My rooks on d5 and d7 defend each other and the d5 rook controls the fifth rank, so Black's queen can't win anything there; Rxg7+ fails to Kxg7 since Rd7+ runs into Qxd7, and pawn moves like a5 or h4 just drop material or invite a fatal rook trade (e.g. a5 Rxa5 Rd8 Qe5+ with Rxd5 ideas). So I keep the fortress intact and make a safe waiting move with the king, conceding the loose a4 pawn at worst while heading toward repetition/50-move drawing chances.

I'm in check from the queen on e2 and only have three king moves; Kg3 looks risky as it exposes my king to further checks (Qe5+, Qe1+) with my king in the open, and Kh1 invites Qf1+ ideas. Kg1 is the safest square, keeps my king sheltered with no back-rank weakness, and steers toward the repetition that suits me given Black's extra material.

I'm down material (queen and rook against my two rooks), so the perpetual check cycle is actually my friend — Kg2 invites Qe2+ Kg1 Qe3+ and a draw by repetition. Kf1 and Kh1 give Black extra options like Qe1+/Qf3+ with my king getting dragged into a mating net or losing a rook to a check-and-skewer, so I stay in the safe shuffle.

I'm only allowed king moves here, and with my king so exposed against the queen while my rooks can't safely trade down (any rook swap leaves a lost Q-vs-rook-and-pawns endgame), the perpetual check sequence is my best practical result. Kg1 keeps the king on the safe squares it has already survived on, where Qe1+/Qe3+ just repeat, and I checked that no mating net exists on g1 with the d-file covered.

My rooks need to stay connected and active; Rd4 attacks the black queen on the fourth rank while being defended by the rook on d7, and the two rooks then mutually protect each other (so Qa7 or Qxd4+ just leads to favourable simplification for me). That gains a tempo and avoids the losing trade after Rd8+ or the outright piece loss after Rxg7+, since g7 is not actually covered.

Rxg7+ fails because Kxg7 just drops a rook for a pawn, leaving me a rook against queen and rook. Instead R4d5 attacks the queen with tempo, blocks the fifth rank so she can't come back to e5/d5, and keeps my rook on the seventh defended by the new rook on d5.

Rxg7+ fails simply to Kxg7, leaving one rook against queen and rook, and Rd8+ invites Rxd8 trading into a lost queen-versus-rook ending. Since I'm down material, I'll keep my mutually-defending rooks on the d-file and start the h-pawn: h4-h5-h6 creates real threats against Black's king and my only practical counterplay.

I'm in check on the b6-g1 diagonal and must block or move the king; Rc5 drops the rook to Qxc5+, but Rd4 blocks with the rook protected by Rd7, so Qxd4 Rxd4 wins the queen for a rook. Keeping the rooks doubled and defended is also better than another king shuffle.

My rook on d4 is currently attacked by the queen on b6 along the c5-d4 diagonal, and Rd5 both escapes that and hits the loose f5 pawn while staying protected by Rd7. Rd8+ fails to Qxd8, and Rxg7+ just drops a rook for a pawn, so keeping the doubled rooks active on the d-file with Rd7 pinning down g7 is my best practical chance.

Any rook trade leaves me with a lone rook against the queen, and Rxf5 drops a rook to Qb1+/Qe4+ forking my split rooks, so I keep my rooks mutually defended on the d-file. h5 is a useful waiting move that preserves the connection and prepares h6 to poke at Black's king shelter for counterplay.

My rooks on d4/d5 defend each other, so any move of the d5 rook (other than a check) drops d4 to Qxd4+ — that rules out Rxf5 and Rd7. Rd8+ forces a rook trade into a lost Q vs R ending, so instead I play h6 to attack g7, fix Black's kingside, and open lines around his king for future rook perpetual-check chances while keeping my rook battery intact.

Rxf5 and Re5 lose a rook to Qxd4 (the d4 rook would be undefended), and Rd8+ forces a trade into a lost queen-versus-rook ending, so I need to keep my rooks connected on the d-file. Rd6 does exactly that — it keeps d4 protected while attacking the queen on b6 and gaining a tempo, since Qxd6 Rxd6 would leave me with rook and pawn against a lone rook.

I'm down material (two rooks vs queen and rook), so I want my rooks mutually defended rather than loose — any move like Rb6 or Rc6 just drops a rook to Qxb6/Rxc6, and Rd8+ Rxd8 Rxd8+ Qxd8 leaves me with nothing. Doubling with R4d5 keeps both rooks protecting each other, attacks the f5 pawn, and preserves my cramping h6 pawn while my king still has air.

Blocking with Rd1 just trades into a hopeless queen-versus-rook ending, so I must move the king; on h2 my d6-rook would be permanently pinned by the queen on the b8–h2 diagonal, and f2 invites Qb6+ followed by Rf1+ with a dangerous attack. On g2 the only pin try is Qb7 along b7–g2, which I answer with Rd7! hitting the queen while still defending d5, and my rooks stay coordinated with the strong h6 pawn.

I'm material down, so I need activity and to remove Black's assets; Rxf5 snatches the extra pawn, keeps my cramping h6 pawn, and the rook is safe (Rc5 is met by Rxc5). If Black replies Qb7+ exploiting the vacated d5, I simply block with Rd5, which is defended by the rook on f5.

I'm in check from Rc2 and my d6 rook is simultaneously hanging to Qxd6 along the b8-h2 diagonal, so passive king moves just drop a rook for nothing. Rd2 blocks but leaves the rook undefended (Rxd2+ wins it outright), whereas Rf2 blocks the check and attacks the black rook, so I either trade rooks on f2 or recapture on c2 after Qxd6.

Blocking with Rc6 or Rd5 just loses a rook to Qxc6/Qxd5, and Kh2/Kh3/Kf1 abandon the f2 rook (Rxf2 wins material cleanly), so I need a square that both escapes the a8-h1 check and keeps f2 guarded. Kg3 does that but walks into Rc3+ and Qa3+ with an exposed king, whereas Kg1 keeps the fortress-like setup with the rooks defending each other.

I'm in check from Rc1, and both Rd1 and Rf1 invite a rook trade that would strip my last defenders and leave me helpless against the queen. Kh2 steps out of check while keeping both rooks active and my h6 pawn cramping Black's king, so the two rooks can keep fighting the queen.
Only one legal move is available — the rook check on h1 forces my king to g3, since Kxh1 isn't legal and nothing can block or capture. I play it and will look to use my rooks actively afterwards.

Kh2 loses a rook to Rxf2 (f2 would be undefended), Kh4 runs into Qd8+ picking off the d6 rook, and Rg2 forces a rook trade into a lost queen-versus-rook ending. Kf4 exposes my king in the open, so I'll step to h3, keeping both rooks protected/active; if Black tries Qg2+ I simply take with Rxg2, and Rh1+ Kg3 just repeats.

I'm down heavy material, so I need the most resilient move; Rf3 and Rd3 both block the check but are simply captured by the queen on the third rank (Qxf3+/Qxd3+ with check), while Kh4 invites g5+ opening my king. Kh2 steps out of check and, crucially, attacks the undefended rook on g1, forcing Black to spend a tempo saving it.
